newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Perry seeks anti-Iraq alliance but doubts grow.
newsitem.headline: Perry seeks anti-Iraq alliance but doubts grow.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry tried to win support for a possible military showdown with Iraq on visits to three Gulf Arab states but doubts surfaced over the wisdom of more strikes at President Saddam Hussein.

Diplomats said Saudi Arabia, Washington's most powerful Gulf ally and one of the three countries Perry visited, was unlikely to back more attacks against Iraq or give open approval for a continuing American military buildup in the oil-rich region.
"If the United States retaliates once more against Iraq without serious provocation I don't think it would be understood by the international community," a senior Western diplomat in Kuwait said.

The latest crisis between the United States and Iraq started 15 days ago. Washington punished Iraq for intervening in the faction fighting in its Kurdish north by launching 44 cruise missiles at air defence systems in southern Iraq last week.
Perry flew into the Saudi Red Sea port of Jeddah on Sunday on his second trip to the kingdom and met King Fahd after visits to Kuwait and Bahrain.

Saudi Defence Minister Prince Sultan bin Abdul-Aziz said he did not expect a new U.S. strike against Iraq after Baghdad's decision announced on Friday to suspend air defence attacks on U.S. and allies warplanes.
Asked if he expected a military confrontation between the United States and Iraq after the Iraqi move, Prince Sultan told reporters on Sunday: "No. I do not think so."

His remarks appeared to echo U.S. ambassador Madeleine Albright who said in the United States Washington would not be pressed into "overreacting" to Iraq, and Iraq appeared unlikely to do anything that would provoke a new U.S. attack.
But in Kuwait Perry dismissed Iraq's pledge to abandon attacks on warplanes patrolling southern and northern no-fly zones, saying: "We cannot rely on Saddam Hussein's promises."

Analysts said they expected Perry to restate the case to the Saudis for containing an unrepentant Iraq six years after it invaded and occupied Kuwait. Gulf Arab states spent tens of billions of dollars to fund the U.S.-led multinational coalition that ejected Iraqi troops from Kuwait in the Gulf War.
Saudi Arabia, eager thus far not to appear as being directly involved in the current U.S. military buildup in the Gulf, has so far kept silent about Perry's visit.
Prince Sultan said on Wednesday that, if asked, Saudi Arabia would have refused to allow U.S. planes already deployed on Saudi bases to be used for raids on Iraq.
In Bahrain Perry said Iraq had rebuilt air defence units and fired six missiles at U.S. warplanes since U.S. missile strikes against Iraq in early September.
He said Washington would send 23 F-16 warplanes to Bahrain "as part of the military force we have in this area, generally that is providing security and stability for the whole region."
Within days, the force is scheduled to include two aircraft carriers with a total of more than 150 Navy aircraft and over 20 other warships and submarines, many armed with cruise missiles.

In Kuwait, the only Arab state to support openly the American show of force, Perry said the United States "will take whatever action is necessary" to enforce an expanded southern Iraqi no-fly zone and to protect U.S. pilots patrolling it.
Asked if more U.S. strikes against Iraq were still possible, Perry told a news conference: "Yes it is still a possibility."
Perry asked Kuwait for permission to proceed with a U.S. plan announced on Friday to deploy several thousand more U.S. troops in the Gulf state. Kuwait is studying the request.
